title: PURSUE: the Pentagon's rolling UAP file releases
agency: US Department of War (Defense), with ODNI, FBI, CIA, NASA, State Department and others
summary: After a presidential order in February 2026, the Department of War began posting declassified UAP records on war.gov in batches every few weeks. Six tranches went up between May 8 and September 18, 2026: Project Blue Book files and films, FBI and CIA memos, State Department cables, NASA mission records, AAWSAP research papers and modern military sensor videos.
why: The largest single government push to publish UFO material since Blue Book closed. Unlike AARO's reports, it deliberately posts unresolved cases and invites outside analysis.
size: 450 records in 6 tranches (270 PDFs, 134 videos, 30 images, 16 audio)

title: UAP Records Collection opens at the National Archives (Record Group 615)
summary: The 2024 defence bill (NDAA FY2024, section 1841) ordered every federal agency to find its UFO and UAP records and hand copies to the National Archives. NARA created a new record group, RG 615, to hold them. By 2026 it had nine series from the FAA, Pentagon, ODNI, NSA, FBI, State Department, Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Customs and Border Protection and the Air Force.
why: For the first time there is one permanent, public home for UFO records from across the US government, with full-text PDFs online.

title: FAA pilot UAP reports (RG 615)
summary: Hundreds of short incident reports from the FAA's Washington Operations Center and its Skywatch system: an airliner or business jet crew radios air traffic control about lights, orbs or objects, and the FAA logs the callsign, aircraft type, altitude, position and what was seen. Many note whether radar saw anything and a few say the lights matched Starlink satellites.
why: The most detailed set of modern pilot sightings ever released, with exact positions for most of them. We've mapped every one.

title: Pentagon and AARO records (RG 615)
agency: Office of the Secretary of Defense / AARO
summary: AARO's own paperwork transferred to the Archives: case resolutions such as Go Fast, Puerto Rico and the Eglin object, the Oak Ridge analysis of a claimed metal fragment, papers on parallax and Starlink flares, briefing slides, hearing transcripts and the annual reports.
why: Shows how the Pentagon's UAP office actually works a case, in its own working documents.

title: NSA records on UFOs (RG 615)
summary: A mixed bag the NSA turned over: State Department airgrams about sightings in Angola, Tunisia and Antarctica, the Joint Chiefs report on the 1976 Tehran jet chase, a Guantanamo sighting report, NSA Technical Journal essays on talking to extraterrestrials, and court papers from a 1980 lawsuit against the agency.
why: Puts the 1976 Iran incident report and the NSA's long-rumoured UFO holdings into the open archive.

title: State Department UFO cables (RG 615)
summary: Diplomatic cables from embassies reporting local UFO stories: lights over the eastern Caribbean, a strange glow over Kuwait, pilots in Tajikistan, sightings in Argentina and Afghanistan, and a Moscow cable headed "UFOs over Georgia".
why: A window on how US diplomats reported other countries' flaps back to Washington.

title: Nuclear Regulatory Commission UAP and drone records (RG 615)
summary: Briefings and emails on how nuclear plants should report drones and UAP flying over them, including a chain about drone sightings near the Pilgrim plant in Massachusetts.
why: Objects over nuclear sites are a recurring theme in UFO history. These show how the regulator handles them today.

title: Customs and Border Protection UAP videos (RG 615)
summary: Twelve sensor videos recorded by CBP aircraft between 2013 and 2021, released as files labelled "Video pertaining to Unidentified Aerial Phenomenon" 1 to 10.
why: Raw footage from a border agency, not the Navy, which most UAP video has come from.

title: Department of the Air Force UFO records (RG 615)
summary: Unit histories and correspondence that mention UFOs: the 1947 MacDill Field history, 4602d Air Intelligence Service Squadron histories, the 1948 "Estimate of the Situation", Curtis LeMay papers, Fifth Air Force intelligence summaries and Air Force Regulation 200-2.
why: Fills gaps around Blue Book with the Air Force's wider paper trail from its early saucer years.

title: FBI Guardian UAP case files (RG 615)
summary: Recent FBI tip files: a report of UAP seen by Anoka, Minnesota police, and possible UAP hovering near a site in the 2024 drone wave, with an FD-302 interview form.
why: Shows the Bureau still logs UFO reports, decades after the famous Hottel memo.

title: ODNI UAP reports (RG 615)
agency: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
summary: Archival copies of the four intelligence community UAP reports: the 2021 preliminary assessment, the 2022 annual report and the FY2023 and FY2024 consolidated reports.
why: The reports Congress asked for, now permanently preserved.

title: AARO FY2025 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
summary: AARO's fourth yearly report to Congress, published months after its deadline. It logs 319 new reports, closes hundreds of older ones, and credits a large share of sightings to sunlight glinting off satellites, using new 3D modelling tools.
why: The latest official count. Every case AARO solved had an ordinary explanation, but most reports still lack enough data to judge.

title: FY2024 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
summary: AARO received 757 reports in the year, 392 of them from the FAA. It resolved dozens as balloons, birds, drones and satellites, flagged 21 for deeper study, and archived 444 for lack of data. Reports near nuclear sites and from US forces over East Asian seas are broken out.
why: The first report to fold in years of FAA pilot data, and the one that put the total past 1,600 reports.

title: AARO Historical Record Report, Volume 1
summary: Congress asked AARO to review the government's entire UFO history. Volume 1 walks through Blue Book, the Robertson Panel, the Condon study, AAWSAP and AATIP, and claims of crashed craft and reverse engineering, and finds no evidence that any government programme recovered alien technology.
why: The Pentagon's official answer to the "secret crash retrieval" claims made in Congress in 2023. Plenty of people dispute it.

title: FY2023 Consolidated Annual Report on UAP
summary: AARO's first full-year report. It received 291 new reports, most of lights or round objects at altitude, bringing the running total to 801. Many were later matched to balloons, drones and clutter.
why: Set the pattern for later reports: lots of sightings, a growing pile resolved as ordinary objects, and a stubborn remainder short on data.

title: AARO case resolution reports
summary: Short write-ups explaining individual cases: the Navy's Go Fast video, the 2013 Puerto Rico object, "Southeast Asia triangles", "atmospheric wakes", a Western United States sighting, an Eglin AFB object, a Mount Etna object and an Al Taqaddum object in Iraq. Each shows the imagery and AARO's explanation.
why: The clearest look at AARO's method. You can check its reasoning against the footage.

title: NASA UAP Independent Study Team report
summary: NASA asked 16 outside experts how science could study UAP. Their report says the main problem is poor data, recommends better sensors, citizen reporting apps and less stigma, and finds no evidence of extraterrestrial origin. NASA named its first director of UAP research the same day.
why: The first time NASA formally weighed in since the 1960s, treating UAP as a data problem worth solving.

title: 2022 Annual Report on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena
agency: Office of the Director of National Intelligence
summary: The follow-up to the 2021 assessment. It added 366 reports, 247 of them new, for a total of 510. About half were tentatively matched to balloons, drones or clutter; 171 stayed uncharacterised, and a few appeared to show unusual flight.
why: Showed that once pilots were encouraged to report, the numbers jumped.

title: Preliminary Assessment: Unidentified Aerial Phenomena
agency: Office of the Director of National Intelligence (UAP Task Force)
summary: A nine-page unclassified report to Congress on 144 military UAP reports. Only one was explained (a deflating balloon). In 18 incidents observers described objects that seemed to move without visible propulsion, and there were 11 near misses with aircraft.
why: The first time the US intelligence community said in public that UAP are real objects, mostly unexplained, and a flight safety issue.

title: Navy UAP videos: FLIR, Gimbal and GoFast
summary: The Pentagon formally released three infrared videos taken by Navy F/A-18 crews, one from the 2004 Nimitz "Tic Tac" encounter and two from 2015 off the East Coast. They had leaked in 2017; the release confirmed they were real and unclassified.
why: These clips restarted mainstream interest in UFOs and led directly to the UAP Task Force, ODNI reports and AARO.

title: House hearing: Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency
agency: House Oversight, Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets
summary: Chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, the task force heard from Air Force veterans, a police chief who saw a UAP, journalist George Knapp and a whistleblower-law expert about sightings and how AARO handles them.
why: Kept congressional pressure on the Pentagon months before the 2026 PURSUE releases.

title: Senate Armed Services open hearing with AARO's director
agency: Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Emerging Threats and Capabilities
summary: AARO director Jon Kosloski briefed senators in public on the FY2024 report and walked through example cases with slides, including ones AARO could not yet explain.
why: Shows AARO presenting unresolved footage to Congress, not just solved cases.

title: House hearing: UAP, Exposing the Truth
summary: Retired Rear Admiral Tim Gallaudet, former AATIP official Luis Elizondo, journalist Michael Shellenberger and former NASA official Michael Gold testified about alleged hidden UAP programmes and called for disclosure.
why: The second big public hearing built around whistleblower claims.

title: House hearing: UAP, Implications on National Security (Grusch hearing)
agency: House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security
summary: Former intelligence officer David Grusch testified under oath that the US has a long-running programme to retrieve crashed craft and "non-human biologics". Navy pilots David Fravor (Tic Tac) and Ryan Graves described their encounters.
why: The most-watched UFO hearing ever, and the reason AARO's historical review and later PURSUE releases happened.

title: Senate hearing on AARO's mission and budget
agency: Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Emerging Threats and Capabilities
summary: AARO's first director, Sean Kirkpatrick, gave senators an open briefing, showing a video of an orb over the Middle East and saying the office had found no evidence of extraterrestrial activity.
why: AARO's public debut in Congress.

title: House Intelligence hearing on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena
agency: House Intelligence Subcommittee on Counterterrorism, Counterintelligence and Counterproliferation
summary: Under Secretary of Defense Ronald Moultrie and Deputy Director of Naval Intelligence Scott Bray testified in public and showed two short Navy clips, one of which they could not explain.
why: The first open congressional hearing on UFOs in more than 50 years.

title: FBI Vault: UFO files and the Hottel memo
summary: The FBI's online reading room includes its 1940s and 1950s flying-saucer file and a one-page 1950 memo from agent Guy Hottel passing on a third-hand story about three saucers and small bodies recovered in New Mexico. The memo became the most viewed page in the Vault.
why: The Hottel memo is endlessly shared as "proof". The FBI itself says it was an unverified tip it never investigated.

title: CIA reading room: "UFOs: Fact or Fiction?"
summary: The CIA's online reading room gathers its declassified UFO documents into one collection: memos from the early 1950s, the Robertson Panel papers, foreign sighting reports and analysis of the U-2 and OXCART spy planes that were often mistaken for UFOs.
why: Shows the CIA's real interest was intelligence and public panic, not little green men, and that its own spy planes caused many sightings.

links.name: Gerald Haines, CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs, 1947-90 (PDF)

title: The Roswell Report: Case Closed
summary: The Air Force's second Roswell report tackled stories of alien bodies. It traced them to crash-test dummies dropped from high-altitude balloons in the 1950s and to real accidents, including a 1956 KC-97 crash, which witnesses may have merged with 1947 in memory.
why: The government's last word on Roswell until AARO. Critics point out the dummies were dropped years after 1947.

title: Report of Air Force Research Regarding the "Roswell Incident"
summary: Prompted by a congressional records search, the Air Force concluded that the 1947 Roswell debris came from Project Mogul, a then-secret string of balloons and radar reflectors meant to listen for Soviet nuclear tests.
why: The first official admission that the 1947 "weather balloon" story was a cover for something classified, just not a spacecraft.

title: GAO: Results of a search for records on the 1947 Roswell crash
summary: At Rep. Steven Schiff's request, Congress's auditors searched government files for Roswell records. They found that key Roswell Army Air Field administrative and outgoing message records from 1945 to 1949 had been destroyed without a recorded authority.
why: The missing records are still a cornerstone of Roswell theories.

title: Project Blue Book case files
summary: The Air Force investigated 12,618 sightings before closing Blue Book in December 1969; 701 stayed unidentified. The declassified files went to the National Archives, which now has 10,622 case folders scanned online.
why: Still the biggest official UFO archive in the world. We've mapped every folder.

title: Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects (the Condon Report)
agency: University of Colorado for the US Air Force
summary: An Air Force-funded study led by physicist Edward Condon concluded that further UFO research was unlikely to advance science. The National Academy of Sciences endorsed it, and the Air Force used it to justify shutting Blue Book.
why: It ended official US UFO investigation for decades. Several of its own case studies stayed unexplained, which critics never let go.

title: House Symposium on Unidentified Flying Objects
agency: House Committee on Science and Astronautics
summary: Six scientists, including J. Allen Hynek, James McDonald and Carl Sagan, gave Congress their views on whether UFOs deserved serious study. Written papers from others were added to the record.
why: Congress heard scientists argue both sides months before the Condon Report closed the door.

title: Robertson Panel report
summary: In January 1953 a CIA-convened panel of scientists led by H.P. Robertson reviewed the best Air Force cases and films. It found no threat and no new physics, and recommended a public education campaign to take the mystery out of UFOs. A cleaned-up version came out in 1958.
why: Often cited as the start of official debunking policy.

title: Ministry of Defence UFO files at The National Archives
agency: Ministry of Defence / The National Archives
summary: From 2008 to 2013 the MoD transferred its UFO desk files to The National Archives in ten batches and they were put online free. They hold public sighting reports, letters, parliamentary questions, Rendlesham Forest papers and internal briefings, ending when the desk closed in 2009.
why: The most complete national UFO file release outside the US, and a running record of what Britons reported for half a century.
reuse: Crown copyright, Open Government Licence (images excluded)

title: UK UFO files: final tranche
agency: Ministry of Defence / The National Archives
summary: The last 25 files, about 4,400 pages, covering the MoD UFO desk's final two years, including the decision to close it in late 2009 because sightings had no defence value.
why: Closes the official British story.

title: Project Condign: UAP in the UK Air Defence Region
summary: A secret study completed in 2000, released under Freedom of Information in 2006. It analysed about 10,000 sighting reports, found no threat, and suggested most unexplained cases were natural atmospheric plasmas, a theory that drew heavy criticism.
why: Britain's equivalent of the Condon Report, kept secret for six years.

title: Canada's UFOs: The Search for the Unknown
summary: Library and Archives Canada digitised the UFO records of the Department of National Defence, Transport Canada, the National Research Council and the RCMP and made them searchable by place and date. They include the 1967 Falcon Lake and Shag Harbour files.
why: Every federal UFO record Canada filed in the Cold War years, scanned and free to read.
reuse: Non-commercial reproduction only (LAC terms); we link rather than copy

title: Sky Canada Project report
agency: Office of the Chief Science Advisor of Canada
summary: A review of how Canada handles UAP reports. It estimates 600 to 1,000 sightings a year with no single body collecting them, and recommends a federal lead, a public reporting service, open data and links with AARO, NASA, GEIPAN and Chile's SEFAA.
why: Canada's first official look at UAP since the National Research Council stopped collecting reports in 1995.

title: GEIPAN opens its case archives
summary: France's official UFO office announced it was putting 30 years of files online: about 1,600 cases, 6,000 witness statements and 100,000 pages. Its website now publishes every investigated case with a grade from A (fully explained) to D (unexplained after investigation), and offers CSV downloads.
why: The model many countries copy: a civilian scientific body that publishes every case and its verdict. Only about 3% end up as D.
reuse: All rights reserved by CNES; extraction prohibited. We link only

title: Brazil's UFO fund at the National Archives
summary: Since 2008 the Air Force has passed its UFO paperwork to the Arquivo Nacional, which holds it as the "Objeto Voador Não Identificado" fund. It includes reports, questionnaires, drawings, photos, audio, and files on the 1986 "official night of UFOs" jet chase and parts of 1977's Operação Prato.
why: One of the largest military UFO archives in Latin America, fully searchable online.
reuse: Public records; licence for bulk reuse not stated. We link only

title: Chile's SEFAA (formerly CEFAA) resolved cases
summary: Chile's civil aviation authority set up a committee to study anomalous aerial phenomena in 1997. Renamed SEFAA in 2022, it publishes regular batches of resolved cases with photos and explanations and released a much-discussed 2014 Navy helicopter video in 2017.
why: One of the few offices worldwide that publishes case verdicts every month.
reuse: Licence not stated. We link only

title: Argentine Air Force CEFAe annual reports
summary: The Air Force's aerospace phenomena commission, set up in 2011, published yearly reports listing each case it studied. The 2015 report found every case it analysed compatible with causes of known origin.
why: A rare set of complete, case-by-case government verdicts.
reuse: Licence not stated. We link only

title: Peru's Air Force reopens its UFO office
summary: The Peruvian Air Force announced it had reopened its Department for the Investigation of Anomalous Aerial Phenomena, closed for five years, and invited the public to send in images and testimony for analysis.
why: Gave Peruvians an official place to send sightings again, with plans to analyse when and where they happen.

title: Mexican Congress public hearing on UAP
summary: A public hearing in Mexico's lower house, organised with journalist Jaime Maussan, heard pilots and researchers, including US Navy veteran Ryan Graves. It became world news when Maussan presented two small mummified bodies he called non-human, a claim scientists widely rejected. A second hearing followed in November 2023.
why: The first UFO hearing in a national legislature outside the US, and a cautionary tale.

title: Italian Air Force UFO sighting lists
summary: Since the 1978 wave, the Italian Air Force has been the official collector of UFO reports. It publishes yearly PDF lists of sightings it could not explain, with place, date, time, shape, colour and duration, plus archives covering 1972 to 2000.
why: A long, steady official series: decades of unexplained sightings, year by year.
reuse: Licence not stated. We link only

title: Spanish Air Force declassified UFO files
agency: Ejército del Aire / Ministerio de Defensa
summary: Between 1992 and 1999 the Spanish Air Force declassified the UFO files it held, covering sightings by its personnel and radars. In 2016 the Defence Ministry put all of them online in its virtual library.
why: Includes classic European cases like the 1979 Manises airliner diversion and the Canary Islands lights.
reuse: Licence not stated. We link only

title: New Zealand Defence Force UFO files
summary: The Defence Force released copies of its UFO files, with names removed, after Archives New Zealand had planned to open them. They hold reports from the public, military personnel and airline passengers, government correspondence and newspaper clippings.
why: Fifty-seven years of what New Zealanders reported to their military, in one set.

title: Australian UFO records at the National Archives
agency: Royal Australian Air Force / National Archives of Australia
summary: The RAAF logged sightings on special report forms for decades. Those files, including reports from the Woomera rocket range, are kept by the National Archives of Australia and many are digitised in its RecordSearch database.
why: Australia's official paper trail, including radar and visual reports from the Woomera weapons range.
